title: Modi Signs a Strategic Partnership in Auckland. Outside the Arena, 300,000 Indian Kiwis Are Living Through a Racism Crisis.
excerpt: India and New Zealand elevated ties to a strategic partnership on Saturday — the first such visit by an Indian PM in 40 years — but the trade deal that brought Modi to Auckland has also unleashed a 'butter chicken tsunami' of anti-Indian backlash.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Modi's visit marks the first by an Indian PM to New Zealand in 40 years.
  • A free trade agreement promises tariff-free access for 57% of New Zealand's exports to India.
  • Anti-Indian sentiment is rising, with incidents of racism reported among the Indian community.
  • 292,000 Indians live in New Zealand, making up 5.5% of the population.
  • Concerns grow that increased migration may exacerbate anti-immigrant sentiment.
The optics were historic. The backdrop was ugly. On Saturday in Auckland, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his New Zealand counterpart Christopher Luxon elevated their bilateral relationship to a "strategic partnership" — a diplomatic upgrade reflecting, in official language, "shared democratic values, deep people-to-people links, and shared interests in the Indo-Pacific." It is the first visit by an Indian prime minister to New Zealand in 40 years. Modi arrived on Friday night after signing deals with Indonesia and Australia on a tour that has taken him across the Asia-Pacific over six days. Later on Saturday, he is expected to address as many as 10,000 members of the Indian diaspora at Auckland's Spark Arena, in what Radio New Zealand has called the centrepiece of the visit. But the celebration is shadowed by something that no communiqué can address: a rising tide of anti-Indian hostility in New Zealand that has made the Indian community a flashpoint in the country's immigration debate. ## 'Butter Chicken Tsunami' The free trade agreement between India and New Zealand, signed in April after negotiations concluded in December 2025, promises expanded market access for both countries. Under the deal, 57 per cent of New Zealand's exports to India will be tariff-free, and provisions covering migration and visas are expected to bring thousands of skilled Indian workers to New Zealand annually. Not everyone is celebrating. Shane Jones, a government minister from the populist New Zealand First party — part of Luxon's ruling coalition — railed against the migration provisions on a local radio show. "I don't care how much criticism we get, I am just never going to agree with a butter chicken tsunami coming to New Zealand," he said, in comments that an Indian community leader called "outright racism." > **"Brian Tamaki, a prominent evangelical preacher and leader of a far-right movement, took to Instagram when he heard Modi was arriving: "Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims."** The backlash went further. Brian Tamaki, a prominent evangelical preacher and leader of a far-right movement, took to Instagram when he heard Modi was arriving: "Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. While we're at it, if they're burning churches down, why don't we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat." New Zealand's race relations commissioner condemned the remarks as "utterly appalling." Earlier this year, Māori activist Che Wilson was accused of insulting Parmjeet Parmar, an Indian-born ACT party MP, with a haka performance that allegedly included mocking references tinged by race. Anti-Indian graffiti has been spray-painted near schools in Auckland, and a far-right group disrupted a Sikh nagar kirtan procession in South Auckland with banners reading "This is New Zealand, not India." These incidents have left many Indian Kiwis feeling vulnerable and questioning their sense of belonging. ![Spark Arena — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Spark_Arena_20220220_131032.jpg/3840px-Spark_Arena_20220220_131032.jpg) ## Defence, Trade, and the Indo-Pacific Beneath the rhetoric, the diplomatic substance is real. Modi and Luxon signed a defence cooperation arrangement and pledged greater collaboration on maritime safety — reflecting shared anxieties about stability in the Indo-Pacific at a time when the Strait of Hormuz crisis has disrupted global energy flows and China's assertiveness in the South China Sea shows no sign of abating. The trade relationship, while still modest by Indian standards, is growing. Bilateral merchandise trade exceeded $1 billion in recent years, though India's exports to New Zealand fell 20 per cent in fiscal year 2026. The FTA is designed to reverse that trajectory, spanning agriculture, services, MSME development, and technical cooperation.
Rising Anti-Indian Sentiment
›292,000 Indian Kiwis in New Zealand, 5.5% of the population.
›Most frequent targets of racially motivated incidents.
›Anti-Indian graffiti reported near schools in Auckland.
›Far-right group disrupted Sikh procession with racist banners.
New Zealand ranks as India's second-largest trading partner in Oceania, after Australia, with which Modi signed a landmark uranium supply agreement earlier this week in Melbourne. ## What It Means for 300,000 Indian Kiwis About 292,000 of New Zealand's 5.3 million people identified as Indian in the 2023 census — a community that has grown rapidly and now makes up roughly 5.5 per cent of the population. That visibility has made them targets. Massey University anthropologist Sita Venkateswar put it bluntly: "A 'butter chicken tsunami', slurs set to a haka, graffiti on a school wall — South Asians are already the most frequent targets of racially motivated incidents in our data. That is real and it is wrong." Many Indian Kiwis have shared stories of increased microaggressions in public spaces and online, with some expressing fear for their children's safety and their own professional prospects. "It feels like we're being told we don't belong, even after contributing to this country for decades," said one Auckland-based IT professional who wished to remain anonymous. Modi's visit is, in part, a signal that New Delhi is paying attention. But for Indian Kiwis living through what many describe as the worst period of anti-Indian sentiment in memory, the strategic partnership signed on Saturday raises a pointed question: whether the economic integration both governments are pursuing will bring the cultural acceptance to match, or whether it will only deepen the resentment. The prospect of increased migration under the FTA, while beneficial for India's economy and skilled workers, also raises concerns among the existing diaspora about how it might exacerbate anti-immigrant sentiment. For the broader Indian diaspora — including the millions in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia who have watched similar cycles of welcome-then-backlash play out in their own countries — New Zealand is not an outlier. It is a mirror, reflecting the ongoing challenge of integration and the need for stronger protections against xenophobia, particularly as global economic ties deepen.

Luxon, for his part, has tried to project warmth. "This visit is about celebrating a winning partnership between New Zealand and India — one that delivers for our people and supports greater prosperity and security for both our countries," he said. Whether the country's 300,000 Indian residents feel that winning partnership in their daily lives is another matter entirely.
